results.title: Hiding Virtualization From Other Software
results.author: Bryan Cockfield
results.content:
The Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) allows Linux systems to function as hypervisors without needing any extra software, but VMs created with it don’t behave exactly like real hardware does. Sometimes that’s important, though, so [sandwich] built a tool called vfio-native that obscures the fact that software might be running in a virtual machine.
There are plenty of the ways that virtual hardware differs from bare metal. The VM may behave slightly differently for obscure instructions in ways that are measurable, it may take slightly longer to perform some tasks, or the hypervisor may simply announce itself directly. vfio-native includes some kernel patches that solve some bugs which address the different behaviors, changes the way that the kernel identifies itself, and attempts to force the CPUs to behave in ways that real hardware would behave. With all of this applied to the virtual machine, it scores a 1/85 against a VM detection tool, with a standard KVM virtual machine scoring 10/85.
For anyone looking to test this out, it’s available in the AUR for Arch Linux. Also, it’s probably worth mentioning that there are more reasons to use this than cheating at Counter-Strike. For example, security researchers testing malware need to know how that software behaves when it thinks its on real hardware, and some may behave in benign ways when confined to virtual machines. Some licensed software also may disable itself when it detects its running in a VM, which can be a nuisance for things like software controlling industrial tools which only run on operating systems that are no longer maintained or hardware that can’t be found anymore. Some other tools we’ve seen before perform similar tasks as well.
results.summary:
The new vfio-native tool modifies Linux Kernel-based Virtual Machine environments to mimic bare-metal hardware, significantly reducing the ability of software to detect that it is running inside a virtual machine.

### Key Points
- The vfio-native tool applies kernel patches to obscure virtual machine signatures and force CPU behavior to match physical hardware.
- Standard KVM virtual machines score 10/85 on detection tests, while systems using vfio-native achieve a score of 1/85.
- The software is currently available for users to install via the Arch User Repository (AUR).
- Security researchers use the tool to observe malware behavior that might otherwise remain dormant when detecting a virtualized environment.
- The tool helps run legacy industrial software that often fails to operate when it identifies a virtual machine host.

### Why it Matters
This development provides a critical solution for researchers and engineers who need to bypass restrictive hardware-detection checks in legacy or security-sensitive applications. By masking virtualization, it ensures that software functions consistently across both physical and virtualized infrastructure.

results.title: California’s billionaire tax faces a precarious road from rich opposition
results.author: Saumya Roy
results.content:
San Francisco, United States – University of California at Berkeley economics professor Brian Galle recently found a flyer in his mailbox about the proposed billionaire tax he helped write. But as he read it, Galle found things he hadn’t written, including that the tax can be on anyone and even on their retirement savings.
Californians have been getting such flyers and watching similar ads as they prepare to vote in the November 3 election on whether to impose the one-time tax of 5 percent on the assets of the state’s billionaires.
Spending by the billionaires to oppose the tax has made this the most expensive ballot measure ever and among the most expensive campaigns of this midterm, says David McCuan, professor of political science at Sonoma State University, who tracks state and local elections.
California’s celebrated tech billionaires, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Doordash founder Tony Xu, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, Ripple co-executive chairman Chris Larsen and venture capitalists John Doerr, Michael Moritz and Vinod Khosla, are among those who have donated more than $300m to block the additional tax on their assets.
While Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg has not donated money to oppose the tax, Meta’s SEC filings revealed that he told the company’s board, which includes Xu and Collison, that he would buy a home outside California to avoid paying the tax. This could have affected Meta stock prices and the board created a new class of shares that Zuckerberg could use to pay the tax.
The billionaire fundraising has far outstripped that of the supporters, who only raised $32m. This has led to the ubiquitous ad campaign as well as outreach to voters.
“I feel like I am in an Alice in Wonderland alternate reality,” said Ashley Craig, a volunteer for Patriotic Millionaires, a group that supports the tax.
Craig has spent months door knocking and making calls to voters to campaign for the tax and often hears misinformation about it.
“They often tell me it has secret provisions allowing everyone to be taxed, which is not entirely true,” she said.
Any change in the tax would require a two-thirds majority in the assembly and would need to stay true to the spirit of the tax. But the prevalence of the ads has meant that voters often tell Craig the tax would soon include her – and them.
Making democracy more equal
“The irony is that Prop 40 [the billionaire tax proposal] is meant to make democracy more equal, but the billionaires are using their money to avoid that,” says Galle, the proposal’s coauthor.
The US Supreme Court’s judgement in the Citizens United v FEC case gave companies and special groups the freedom to spend freely in elections, he said.
“This has led to this situation where Sergey Brin has a lot more of a political voice,” says Francesco Trebbi, the BT Rocca professor of Business and Public Policy at the University of California at Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “It’s Sergey Brin v millions of Californians. This leads people to lose trust in the system ” .
Apart from the ad buys, Craig says she has also felt alone in the campaign arena. While the state Democratic party has endorsed the tax proposal, Craig says she hasn’t had ground support from the party. “We don’t have resources like social media, door knocking, phone banking and I would place the blame at the feet of the Democratic party.”
Sonoma State’s McCuan attributes this to the Democratic party’s internal rift between the progressives and moderates, with the former in favour of such a policy and the latter resisting it.
“This is a broader proxy test between the party’s progressives and moderates. If this works, progressive candidates could try such ideas in the 2028 presidential elections,” McCuan says, which the billionaires and moderates want to avert.
So while the party has endorsed the measure, California Governor Gavin Newsom has opposed it, as has Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor in the election and Katie Porter, a former congresswoman who also ran for governor.
Newsom, who is eyeing a 2028 presidential run, has opposed the tax, saying it is “poorly written. It would harm the state if its billionaires, who have an estimated wealth of 2.3 trillion according to the measure’s authors, move, as Zuckerberg has planned,” Newsom has said.
The tax’s opponents have also backed a ballot measure that prohibits any new state taxes based on personal property or imposed retroactively. Another asks state auditors to review any proposed tax measures for their financial impact before they are voted on. If these pass and get more votes than the billionaire tax, they could negate the billionaire tax, even if it is passed.
Only a third of citizen initiatives pass
The strong campaign opposing the billionaire tax may have impacted support for it. Voters support the tax by a small margin, but also the two measures that oppose it, according to a recent poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC).
“Only about a third of such citizen initiatives pass. So the burden is on the yes side,” says Mark Baldassare, statewide survey director and Miller chair in public policy at PPIC. “Support can decline if people don’t feel completely sure.”
But Suzane Jiminez, chief of staff at the SEIU health workers union, which has sponsored the billionaire tax measure, said, “We are feeling confident that we will have the votes. When voters see that billionaires are funding the ads, they see through them.”
Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Congressman Ro Khanna of California rallied across the state to drum up support for the measure. Jiminez said that in the last few weeks, 3,000 volunteers have spread out to knock on doors and distributed flyers explaining the tax across the state. “The democratic figureheads do not represent the rank and file on this. They are supporting us,” Jiminez said.
It is unclear whether this will be enough, as the shortfall in funding means support for the measure remains precarious. Baldassare said he plans to do his poll again as voters read and receive the state’s voter guides explaining the ballot measures and make up their minds.
Sonoma University’s McCuan said that just the historic amount of money being spent on defeating the measure is a win in itself for the tax backers.
“Progressives can win by losing. They can say moderates sank us, use it as a morality play. They will attack big tech – as a bad bogeyman of US politics.”
results.summary:
California voters are deciding on a proposed five percent tax on billionaire assets, a ballot measure that has become the most expensive campaign in state history.

### Key Points
- Tech billionaires, including Sergey Brin and Tony Xu, have donated over $300 million to defeat the proposed tax on their assets.
- Supporters of the measure have raised only $32 million, leading to a significant disparity in advertising and voter outreach efforts.
- Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg reportedly considered moving out of California to avoid the tax, prompting the company to create a new share class.
- Opponents have introduced competing ballot measures that could legally negate the billionaire tax if they receive more votes.
- California Governor Gavin Newsom and other prominent Democrats oppose the measure, citing concerns that it is poorly written and could drive wealth out of the state.

### Why it Matters
This campaign highlights a growing political divide between progressive and moderate factions within the Democratic Party regarding wealth taxation and corporate influence. The outcome serves as a high-stakes test for future economic policies and demonstrates how massive private spending can shape public perception of ballot initiatives.

results.title: Cybersecurity CEO Indicted for Allegedly Scamming Millions From Ransomware Victims
results.author: Renee Dudley
results.content:
A Florida man who was the subject of a 2019 investigation by ProPublica was indicted last month on federal charges that he defrauded clients of his ransomware data recovery firm.
According to the Justice Department, the man, Zohar Pinhasi, told customers he could recover their encrypted files without having to pay hackers, when, in reality, he paid the ransom and charged victims a hefty fee on top.
The indictment mirrors the findings from ProPublica’s 2019 article “The Trade Secret,” which centered on Pinhasi and his scheme. The outlet found that the ransomware victims were being harmed twice: once by the hackers, who locked their targets’ files and demanded ransom, and a second time by MonsterCloud, Pinhasi’s Florida-based data recovery firm, which misled its clients about not paying ransoms.
“By falsely claiming to decrypt ransomware without paying off the ransomers, the defendant re-victimized his clients while extracting a hefty profit for himself,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said in an Oct. 7 press release. “Our Office will vigorously prosecute ransomware attackers who prey on Americans from across the world and those who cynically profit from their criminal activity.”
When ProPublica published its story in 2019, ransomware was growing into one of the world’s most pervasive cyberthreats. Hackers locked the data of governments, schools and businesses, holding the decryption key for a ransom payment, which they usually demanded in bitcoin and other types of difficult-to-trace cryptocurrency.
ProPublica’s reporting focused on how U.S. industries, from data recovery firms like MonsterCloud to insurance giants that cover ransom payments, all fueled the extortion economy. Ransomware remains a widespread threat today, and the threat to national security has grown as hackers linked to hostile foreign governments are believed to use ransomware as a cover for espionage. The prevalence of AI tools is also making it easier for attackers to spread ransomware.
Pinhasi, who went by the alias Zack Green, told ProPublica in 2019 that MonsterCloud never promised clients that their data will be recovered by any particular method. “How we do it, it’s our problem,” he told ProPublica. “You will get your data back. Sit back, relax and enjoy the ride.” He called MonsterCloud’s data recovery methods a “trade secret.”
Pinhasi hung up when reached on his cellphone this month. A message left with a representative at MonsterCloud’s office phone number and a message left with his attorney were not returned. A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Pinhasi pleaded not guilty to the federal charges.
In its 2019 investigation, ProPublica interviewed MonsterCloud’s clients and ransomware experts and found that in certain cases the firm must have paid ransoms on behalf of clients. MonsterCloud’s services were particularly popular with local law enforcement agencies, who are loath to engage with or pay criminal hackers. Several interviewed by ProPublica at the time said they chose MonsterCloud to help them recover from ransomware because they believed the firm would never pay a ransom.
Pinhasi, who described himself to ProPublica as a former IT security intelligence officer for the Israeli military, said in 2019 that MonsterCloud handled up to 30 calls a day and had about 20 employees in South Florida as well as extensive global contacts.
Federal investigators found that, over the course of the scheme, Pinhasi allegedly charged clients more than $19 million and paid more than $8 million in ransom payments. In one example, Pinhasi made a ransom payment of about $8,200 but charged the client about $150,000. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in prison.
In the Justice Department’s October press release, an FBI official said Pinhasi had “turned the victim’s crisis into his own profit center. This deception is unacceptable, and the FBI is committed to ensuring accountability for those who choose to victimize the very people who trusted them for help.”
The Justice Department did not address ProPublica’s 2019 finding that one of the FBI’s own was among Pinhasi’s associates at MonsterCloud. John Pistole, a former deputy director of the FBI under Robert Mueller, was prominently featured in a promotional video on MonsterCloud’s homepage. “Police departments, government agencies, hospitals, small business and Fortune 500 firms trust MonsterCloud to help recover from attacks and protect against new ones,” Pistole said in the video. “MonsterCloud’s proprietary technology and expertise protects their professional reputations and organizational integrity.”
Pistole was not mentioned by name in the Pinhasi indictment.
In 2019, Pinhasi touted MonsterCloud’s ties to law enforcement as evidence of its integrity. Pistole, who also headed the Transportation Security Administration under President Barack Obama, was listed on MonsterCloud’s website as the only member of its “Cyber Security Advisory Council.”
Pistole did not respond to a request for comment for this story. In a 2019 interview, he said he became acquainted with Pinhasi after MonsterCloud reached him through a speaker’s bureau and that MonsterCloud paid him indirectly through that group. He said Pinhasi scripted his testimonial and that he was well aware that in most cases — including MonsterCloud’s — the only way to decrypt data locked by ransomware is to pay the hackers. “That’s the business model as I understood it,” Pistole told ProPublica at the time. “Based on my experience and knowledge, ransom is paid and they facilitate the best practices moving forward.”
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment on Pistole’s connection to MonsterCloud.
results.summary:
Florida-based data recovery firm owner Zohar Pinhasi faces federal charges for allegedly defrauding clients by secretly paying ransoms to hackers while claiming to use proprietary decryption methods.

### Key Points
- Zohar Pinhasi, owner of MonsterCloud, was indicted for allegedly charging clients over $19 million while secretly paying $8 million in ransoms.
- The indictment follows a 2019 ProPublica investigation that exposed the firm for misleading victims about its recovery processes.
- Pinhasi faces up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted of the fraud charges.
- Former FBI deputy director John Pistole previously appeared in promotional materials for MonsterCloud, though he is not named in the current indictment.
- The Justice Department alleges Pinhasi exploited clients' crises for personal profit by falsely claiming he could bypass ransom payments.

### Why it Matters
This case highlights the ethical and legal risks within the growing ransomware recovery industry, where service providers may prioritize profit over transparency. It serves as a warning to organizations that relying on third-party firms to handle cyber extortion can lead to further victimization and financial exploitation.

results.title: Did Substack Fix the Internet?
results.author: Kyle Chayka
results.content:
The question of how to survive as a writer is only slightly older than the impulse to be one in the first place. How to express yourself freely but also to be valued for said expression? Historically, strategies for making ends meet have included seeking religious or royal patronage; producing printed books; serializing your work in publications; and hustling to sell your own subscriptions, as Alexander Pope did when he funded his eighteenth-century translation of the Iliad. The investigative journalist I. F. Stone had his own printed-and-mailed newsletter I.F. Stone’s Weekly, which cost five dollars a year and ran from 1953 to 1971, reaching some seventy thousand subscribers. In more recent years, the go-to option for an aspiring writer has been starting a newsletter of her own, often on Substack, a digital platform that launched in 2017 to allow writers to charge money for their writing. Hamish McKenzie, Substack’s co-founder, argues in a new book (that venerable format!), “How to Save the Media,” that Substack’s ecosystem of individual authors behind personal paywalls has solved the problem of cutting through the social-media cacophony and fulfilled writers’ quest for a livelihood. In McKenzie’s estimation, Substack represents “a better system design that distributes rather than concentrates both power and responsibility.”
McKenzie is a journalist by trade, who spent much of his career covering tech startups. With “How to Save the Media,” he has published something between a memoir and a manifesto, delivered in the quippy tone of twenty-tens blogging. He breezily recounts his life in the media industry, which began when he escaped his youth in small-town New Zealand to study journalism in Canada. After finding fecund ground in the Hong Kong tech scene, he landed in San Francisco during Silicon Valley boom times. He endured stints at such niche publications as PandoDaily before working at Tesla (and, after leaving, wrote a book about the company, leading to clashes with Elon Musk). While working at the messaging app Kik, he met Chris Best, Kik’s chief technology officer and his future Substack co-founder. The two saw that media companies were overly reliant on social media for distribution, and that profits were flowing to the likes of Facebook rather than to the creators of content. They wanted to build “a game where people would happily pay for good media,” scaling up the preëxisting achievements of writers such as Andrew Sullivan and Ben Thompson, whose small digital publications thrived on a subscription model. Substack would help writers publish their content and charge their readers while managing the messy back-end business, in exchange for ten per cent of writers’ revenue.
McKenzie courts for Substack such writerly talents as Bill Bishop, Matthew Yglesias, and Bari Weiss, whose publication The Free Press remains among the most popular and best-earning offerings on the platform. He recounts a boozy literary party sponsored by his company and quotes liberally, and redundantly, from his own old speeches and blog posts. The Substack team fends off acquisition offers from Jack Dorsey’s Twitter and Musk’s X, choosing to prioritize their independence. They also navigate debates over free speech from critics who complain that Substack hosts, and thus profits from, hateful content including pro-Nazi newsletters. McKenzie’s justification is ultimately the same as that of the social networks that he argues against: Substack is a neutral platform empowering its users, not an arbiter of truth. He writes, “When a platform decides what its uses are and aren’t allowed to see, it effectively positions itself as a centralized police force with the moral authority to decide what’s good and what’s bad.”
Such big-tent branding has helped Substack to become an unqualified success, at least in the eyes of its investors, and has made “Substacking” a cultural buzzword, much as “tweeting” dominated the early twenty-tens. It’s not just reporters who have Substacks now; celebrities (Pamela Anderson), musicians (Patti Smith), and traditional publications (including The New Yorker) do, too. (I, full disclosure, have my own accounts.) The rescued “media” of McKenzie’s title encompasses not just journalism but a broader realm of entertainment, with Substack providing a monetizable layer between creators and their fans. The company is, in essence, a crowdfunding e-commerce site, belonging to the same category as Kickstarter, Patreon, Gumroad, and OnlyFans. But it has out-evolved its ancestors and bested its competitors in its relevance to public discourse and in its direct commodification of online parasocial relationships. McKenzie predicts that “new companies will emerge” from such subscription platforms, but thus far Substack has only encouraged further atomization as audiences gravitate toward the loudest, most charismatic voices. The result is not a revived traditional media industry—few Substacks employ editors, for example—so much as a new form of public square in which anyone can shout.
“How to Save the Media” belongs to the genre of instructive founder’s autobiography, in which the heroic entrepreneur inevitably endures some brief trials on his path to power and riches, and offers the business lessons learned along the way. If mass social platforms driven by advertising are what’s wrong with the internet, McKenzie argues, then a platform driven by subscriptions can save it. Substack does allow thousands more writers (and podcasters and miscellaneous creators) to sustain careers in an otherwise barren industry landscape; it is now considered normal to charge your followers’ credit cards the cost of a fancy caffeinated beverage each month for the privilege of receiving your reporting, recipes, or ramblings. Yet as the company has grown, Substack has also come to look more like its stated enemies: it added a Twitter-esque feed of algorithmically recommended short posts, called Notes; its app has become a multimedia hub. McKenzie criticizes social media for how it “turns publishers into digital characters who compete for attention on crowded feeds,” but aspiring writers now hustle to make themselves known as characters on Substack, too. The writer Emily Sundberg, whose newsletter “Feed Me” is one of McKenzie’s highlighted triumphs, observed, in an influential 2024 essay, that “if you blacked out the names of many of the writers I come across on Substack today, I wouldn’t be able to tell them apart.” She went on to pinpoint the Substack generic style: “lists, random thoughts, and (easy to write) roundups of ‘what I’ve been doing’ do really well on this site.”
Another new book, “Content Machines,” by the Carleton University professor Sarah Brouillette, is less optimistic than McKenzie’s about digital platforms’ influence on publishing. In the online marketplace, Brouillette argues that writers have become mercenaries, “a node in a network of needy users” who must “invest their own time and money in design and sales if they want to succeed.” The book proceeds through chapters on such phenomena as the user-generated fiction platform Wattpad, BookTok and the popularity of the romance genre, Audible’s many algorithm-gaming offerings, self-publishing advice gurus, and autofiction’s relationship to social media. In each case, she analyzes how the structures and forces of the various internet platforms shape the style of the writing hosted on them. A roving analyst in addition to a well-read academic, Brouillette pays close attention to the trappings of Wattpad conventions (known as WattCon) and to such textual specimens as “How to Write a Book in 48 Hours,” by the self-publishing coach Dale L. Roberts, which suggests such hacks as using talk-to-text programs or “outsourcing” work to others. She concludes that writing on the internet, particularly in spaces where it’s simple to charge money for it, tends to push writers toward the confessional, the self-helpy, and the soothing.
Though Substack is not one of Brouillette’s subjects, much of what she describes applies equally to the platform—like, say, “a new kind of labor regime that turns people’s daily online creativity into an agglomerated mass of possibly monetizable material.” As content creators struggle to compete for attention and subscription dollars, they end up finding their way to the same solutions, relying on “established patterns,” Brouillette writes, echoing Sundberg’s observation; the goal is less to produce great writing than to “maximize your work’s efficiency.” Social media is blamed for raising a generation of self-promoting narcissists and fuelling a precipitous decline in attention spans and intellectual engagement. But in the new writer economy a “desperation for attention” is practically “an industry command,” Brouillette writes. The platform may not save journalism as a whole, but it certainly helps prolong the careers of those willing to play the “game,” as McKenzie put it, of cultivating their personal brands. ♦
results.summary:
Substack co-founder Hamish McKenzie explores the platform's role in modern media in his new book, detailing how subscription-based models aim to empower writers and decentralize digital content distribution.

### Key Points
- Substack, launched in 2017 by Hamish McKenzie and Chris Best, allows creators to monetize content through direct reader subscriptions.
- The platform takes a 10% revenue share while positioning itself as a neutral host, avoiding the editorial oversight common in traditional media.
- High-profile writers like Bari Weiss and Matthew Yglesias have helped the platform gain significant cultural influence and financial success.
- Critics, including professor Sarah Brouillette, argue that such platforms force writers to prioritize personal branding and content efficiency over traditional journalism.
- Substack has expanded beyond text to include multimedia features like "Notes," increasingly resembling the social media networks it originally sought to disrupt.

### Why it Matters
Substack represents a significant shift in the creator economy by moving media power from centralized advertising-based platforms to individual, subscription-funded authors. While it provides a viable livelihood for many writers, it also risks homogenizing content as creators adapt their work to satisfy algorithmic demands and audience expectations.

results.title: OPPO Find 10 Pro Max review: the best Android phone ever made
results.author: nirave@hot.tech (Nirave Gondhia) , Nirave Gondhia
results.content:
Android Central Verdict
There’s no doubt that Oppo built the most complete Android phone ever made. Oppo has consistently built the best phones for the past two generations, but the Find X10 Pro Max surprised me with how well it performs throughout. All three 200MP cameras are outstanding, the teleconverter kit has seen a huge upgrade thanks to software improvements, and the video recording is as capable as its rivals. The excellence extends beyond the cameras; the 8,000 mAh battery is big enough to act as a power bank and can last for multiple days, with 80W charging and the latest MediaTek internals. The Find X10 Pro Max answers the question: what happens if you put a dream wishlist inside a smartphone? The answer is simple: a best-in-class experience. The best part? It’s launching globally.
Reasons to buy
- + Class-leading triple 200MP camera setup takes outstanding stills and videos
- + Fantastic battery life with 80W charging
- + Vibrant QHD AMOLED with 144Hz refresh
- + The best internals of any phone
- + Improved software in ColorOS 17
- + IP68/IP69 dust and water resistance
- + Launching globally
Reasons to avoid
- - Charging is slightly slower than last year
- - EU models have a smaller battery
- - Eye-watering starting price
- - Won't get as many updates as Google and Samsung phones
Why you can trust Android Central
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
It's hard to emphasize just how good the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is. As a tech journalist for the past 20 years, I've heard many comments wishing a company would just put everything into a phone, and while we've seen that before, no one has done it as successfully as Oppo.
The company's return to global markets comes with a phone that does it all. Most phones have one or two 200MP cameras; the Find X10 Pro Max uses 200MP sensors on all three cameras. Some phones struggle with battery life; the Find X10 Pro Max lasts for days. Some flagships struggle with performance, even when they're high-priced; the MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro inside the Find X10 Pro Max has never faulted during my weeks of use.
This is the Find X10 Pro Max in a nutshell. Oppo made the best phone it could, designed for those who want the best. The Find X10 Pro Max is an Ultra in all but name, but like any phone, it has a few things worth noting.
Normally, it's easy to find flaws when writing a review. However, the Find X10 Pro Max is so good that, aside from a slightly smaller EU battery and discoloration on the included white case, it has only one major downside: its high price, made even higher by the ongoing RAM crisis.
Starting at £1,499 in the UK and €1,799 in Europe, this is amongst the most expensive phones you can buy, at least the non-folding kind. There are some deals, and you can get the excellent Teleconverter Kit for free (worth £500), plus further trade-in discounts, but you'll still pay a sizable price. That said, this phone promises everything and delivers, and although it’s expensive, I think it’s worth it.
The Find X10 Pro Max is the most complete Android phone I've ever used, and it sets an extremely high standard for other companies to match. It has all the hardware you need, ColorOS is my favorite user interface, and Oppo is beefing up its after-sales service alongside six years of updates. If you've ever loved a OnePlus phone, this is the successor you’ve been waiting for, and you'll thoroughly enjoy it.
If you want the best phone that money can buy, look no further than the Find X10 Pro Max. Here’s why it's likely the best Android phone of the year.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
The most complete camera on a smartphone
Our review of the Find X9 Ultra earlier this year said its camera system was on another level entirely, and in six months, Oppo has raised the bar considerably. Yes, the Find X10 Pro Max doesn't have a 1-inch sensor or the secondary telephoto lens, both of which I presume will come in a future Find X10 Ultra, if at all, but it has everything else you want, starting with triple 200MP cameras.
I’ve always wondered what would happen if a company built the first phone with only 200MP cameras. The answer is obvious: you get stunning photos and videos across all three lenses, at various zoom levels, in a variety of conditions. In short, the Find X10 Pro Max camera does it all, and you won't need much else. If you do, the Teleconverter Kit takes it to a new level, making it the best free gift if you can choose.
The main camera uses a 200MP f/1.5 Samsung ISOCELL HPC 1/1.28-inch sensor, co-developed by Oppo and Samsung, paired with a 24mm focal length, phase-detection autofocus, and OIS.
What makes the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max truly unique is its ultrawide and telephoto cameras, both using the same /2.2 200MP Samsung Isocell HP5 1/1.56-inch sensor you’ll find in many phones. It’s smaller than the sensors you might find in other telephoto cameras, but that hasn’t affected telephoto performance. The ultrawide has autofocus, while the telephoto has autofocus, OIS, a 10 cm minimum focal distance, and 3x optical zoom.
In virtually every scene I tested, the Find X10 Pro Max camera excelled. The processing can be somewhat aggressive, especially with sunset hues, but that applied to less than 0.5% of the 1,000 photos and videos that I captured. Thanks to Oppo’s new LUMO True Image Engine and its ongoing, multi-year partnership with Hasselblad, you get fantastic, true-to-color photos across every use case I tried, from landscapes while on a boat in the Spanish sea to capturing portraits of people and pets at a variety of focal lengths in a range of conditions.
The same goes for video recording, with Oppo stacking the Find X10 Pro Max camera to make it ideal for video creators. You can record up to 4K at 60fps, 4K at 120fps, and even 8K at 30 fps. It supports Dolby Vision, ACES-certified O-Log2, and, for the first time on an Oppo smartphone, Open Gate Capture.
This is a big deal for capturing memories: it records in 4:3 and uses the full imaging area, unlike most smartphones that crop the camera sensor, so you can easily reframe between horizontal and vertical videos in editing later. This means you can edit the same video into a widescreen YouTube video or a vertical Instagram Reel without the awkward framing and cropping you’ll find on most phones and cameras.
The Teleconverter will further enhance the camera
What really surprised me about the Find X10 Pro Max is its teleconverter kit. Oppo has struggled to make this stable enough to be reliable in past generations, but this year's teleconverter kit is outstanding.
The kit includes a teleconverter that offers 10x optical zoom, which is also available in the fourth lens on the Find X9 Ultra, plus up to 40x zoom that's surprisingly capable.
The biggest improvement is its stability, especially at 10x and 20x. This is a big step up, especially in video. Previously, I wouldn't have used the teleconverter kit for video, at least not without the tripod mount, but the Find X10 Pro Max changes that; I captured the following video handheld, without a tripod, and it speaks volumes.
The kit also includes a protective case, a tripod adapter ring, a storage bag, and a camera shoulder strap. One downside I noticed: the white protective case shipped with the Luna White phone discolored considerably within a few days.
Priced at £549 in the UK, the Teleconverter Kit isn’t a must-have purchase as the cameras are so capable without it, but it will significantly enhance your experience. It also comes with a beautifully designed soft vegan leather carry pouch, a first for Oppo’s teleconverters and a welcome surprise.
The kitchen sink of smartphone hardware
If you could put together a wishlist for what a smartphone should have, you would inevitably end up with Oppo. They’ve picked up the mantle from companies like Huawei and Samsung in past eras, and the Find X10 Pro Max is the latest in an incredible smartphone lineup.
The Find X9 Ultra is this year’s best Ultra phone, mostly for its 1-inch sensor, but the Find X10 Pro Max performs better thanks to its triple 200MP setup and a more optimized experience in ColorOS 17. Last year, the Find X9 Pro marked the start of Oppo’s new direction and set a standard that the Find X10 Pro Max clearly outperforms, while this year's Find N6 is arguably the year’s best folding phone. With this pedigree, it’s no surprise that the Find X10 Pro Max has everything you could want in a smartphone.
The Dimensity 9600 Pro delivers premium, flagship performance, and with Oppo’s optimizations, I haven't experienced a single slowdown. It’s paired with 12GB or 16GB of RAM and between 256GB and 1TB of storage; my review sample has 16GB and 512GB, respectively. This goes beyond the processor, and I’ve found the network and call performance superb, including while roaming with Google Fi in the UK and with both EE and Fi in Spain. The under-display ultrasonic fingerprint scanner is easy to set up and unlocks extremely fast, but you probably won’t even get to it, since facial unlock is also superb.
It also has an IR scanner, and I love carrying Oppo phones for that reason. On numerous occasions, I’ve used Oppo phones, including the Find X10 Pro Max and Find N6, to bypass locked-down hotel TV remotes or control my Apple TV when I forget the remote and can’t connect via my iPhone. It’s a timely reminder of a use case that’s becoming more frequent: infrared remotes are a good thing that should never have gone away.
Outstanding battery life and efficiency
Oppo is known for large batteries, superfast charging, and incredible battery life, and the Find X10 Pro Max delivers on all three, with a couple of caveats.
First, the global model has an 8,000 mAh battery, but the EU model has a smaller 7,150 mAh capacity. I’m testing the 8,000 mAh model, and it's proven to be an absolute champion, but the EU model will likely offer slightly less battery life. Another point: it’s smaller than last year’s Find X9 Pro, which had a 7,500 mAh battery in the EU.
The global Find X10 Pro Max offers outstanding battery life, among the best in the industry. I haven’t run my full battery benchmark suite yet, so I can’t quantify exactly how much it beats the competition, but it has the best battery life of any flagship I’ve tried. The large capacity and 10W reverse wired or wireless charging also make it a strong emergency power bank, and I’ve used it to charge other devices with strong results: wired charging is straightforward, but aligning devices for wireless reverse charging can be hard. It’ll probably work, but it’s a last resort.
Charging is the other caveat: on paper, it matches other Oppo flagships, but the company has taken a conservative approach, and it’s much slower than previous generations. A full charge takes about 72 minutes, for an average charge rate of 111.11 mAh/minute. Meanwhile, the Find X9 Ultra's 7,050 mAh battery charges to full in about 48 minutes, for a charge rate of 146.88 mAh/min, or ~32% faster.

| Oppo Find X10 Pro Max | 8,000 | 80W | 27% | 53% | 
| Oppo Find X9 Ultra | 7,050 | 80W | 44% | 76% | 
| Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra | 5,000 | 60W | 49% | 83% | 
| Google Pixel 11 Pro XL | 5,115 | 45W | 45% | 77% | 
| Honor Magic 8 Pro | 6,270 | 100W | 46% | 82% | 
This is even more pronounced at the 15- and 30-minute marks. I’ve previously tested the Galaxy S26 Ultra, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Find X9 Ultra, and when I ran the same test on the Find X10 Pro Max, I was surprised it trailed the competition in both.
Notably, these are only 1-2% lower than the Find X9 Pro, so it’s not a major year-on-year downgrade, but it's surprising to see Oppo trail the competition given how far ahead it has been in the past.
Stand-out design and a vibrant display
The Find X10 Pro Max follows a similar design to last year’s Find X9 Pro, though Oppo has extended the camera module horizontally. The key difference is the new Lumo Camera Island, an additional aluminum camera island that houses the True Color Camera and LED flash. Like past Oppo phones, it also has a subtle orange accent that nods to Hasselblad’s iconic camera designs.
In the hand, the Find X10 Pro Max is the most balanced phone I’ve used in years. It feels premium, flagship, and solid, which is exactly what you want from a £1,500 phone. The flat aluminum frame has slightly contoured edges, which make it surprisingly comfortable to grip for extended periods.
The Find X10 Pro Max measures 8.4mm thick and weighs 233 grams. Neither is groundbreaking, but it is thicker and heavier than the Galaxy S26 Ultra. That’s not exactly surprising, as the Find X10 Pro Max is a considerable upgrade. It's also thinner and lighter than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and its weight distribution makes it feel less top-heavy.
The 6.78-inch display is nearly the perfect size for comfortable one-handed use, but it does require some stretching, far less than rival devices with bigger screens. The display is similar to the Find X9 Pro, but it does reach 144Hz. Oppo also says the brightness is slightly higher, and an increased PWM Dimming rate of 3,840Hz should make it easier on people with sensitive eyes.
During its launch and briefings, Oppo specifically called out the bezels around the display. At 1.15mm thick, they’re among the thinnest on any smartphone, for a more immersive viewing experience. This is even better for streaming, with HDR10+, HDR Vivid, and Dolby Vision all supported. In daily use, the screen is excellent in all conditions, and I’ve had no legibility issues, even on the water under overcast sun.
The software has plenty to like
The only issue I have with the software on the Find X10 Pro Max is that it won't get as many software updates as Google and Samsung phones. With a guarantee of five major version updates and six years of security updates, Oppo has improved over the four years offered with the Find X9 Pro, but still lags behind the seven years of updates offered by Google, Motorola, Samsung, and Honor.
I tested the global Find X10 Pro Max model with Android 17-based ColorOS 17 and encountered no issues using any part of the software. Oppo's ColorOS 17 interface is its most refined yet, and it is extremely reliable when using Gemini and Google AI features.
ColorOS is my favorite Android interface right now, as Oppo pairs a smart set of default choices with the ability to customize virtually everything. Most Android makers offer a smart set of defaults, but lack the latter, which is key: the ability to tweak, change, and optimize for your workflow is a throwback to why we love Android.
In my opinion, this is the gold standard of smartphone interfaces, and its ability to integrate and quickly share to other devices, including AirDrop between iPhone and Mac, is also the most polished I've seen on any Android phone.
The Find X10 Pro Max defines what a true flagship is
My biggest takeaway with the Find X10 Pro Max is that it’s hard to find any real faults. It’s rare to call a phone perfect, and while no phone ever is, the Find X10 Pro Max is the closest attempt yet at building the perfect smartphone. A few small negative asides; this review is particularly glowing for a reason: the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is the best Android phone I’ve ever used.
The cameras are the best you’ll find in this class of phone in 2026, only surpassed in certain specific conditions by Oppo’s own Find X9 Ultra. The display is fantastic, battery life is superb, and MediaTek delivers true flagship performance. Add in some neat improvements in ColorOS 17, and you have the leading contender for phone of the year.
The Find X10 Pro Max is also getting Oppo’s largest global Find series release yet, and it will be available in over 60 countries, though the US isn't one of them. That means it’ll compete with the Galaxy S27 Ultra, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and models from Vivo, Honor, and Xiaomi. It’s hard to see how any of those phones will beat Oppo, as the Find X10 Pro Max is just that good.

results.title: Elon Musk confirms $40 billion SpaceX debt deal for AI chips, warns of neocloud shakeout
results.author: Omkar Godbole, AI Boost
results.content:
Elon Musk issues a warning for 'AI neoclouds' as SpaceX borrows $40 billion for chips
SpaceX has raised $40 billion in debt to buy GPUs, while Musk predicts a major shakeout among smaller AI cloud providers.
- SpaceX has raised $40 billion in callable debt to buy GPUs, leveraging its strong credit rating and revenue from Starlink and rocket launches.
- Elon Musk said debt markets have largely closed to companies without substantial revenue beyond AI data centers, and he predicted that more than 200 “neocloud” providers will consolidate into a few survivors.
Nasdaq-listed SpaceX  has raised $40 billion in debt to buy GPUs, the powerful processors used to run artificial-intelligence systems. 
Elon Musk announced the deal on X, pairing it with a warning for neoclouds — companies whose revenue depends almost entirely on data centers — that could add to AI jitters on Wall Street and risk aversion in broader financial markets, including cryptocurrencies.
The $40 billion deal is mainly callable debt, meaning SpaceX can repay it early. The money could be used to pay for GPU deliveries expected in the first half of 2027, though Musk did not explicitly say so. Reuters previously reported that SpaceX was negotiating with banks and asset managers to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia AI chips.
Musk said the reason SpaceX could borrow the money is because it has a strong credit rating and steady revenue from Starlink internet service and rocket launches. Those businesses do not depend on AI data centers, making it easier for SpaceX to secure chip financing than for companies that rely entirely on data centers for revenue. Debt funding for such firms is drying up, Musk noted.
“As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers,” he said on X.
Musk predicted that more than 200 “neoclouds” — newer companies that rent out AI computing power — will consolidate, with only a few surviving.
The episode shows how costly the AI computing race has become. Building large clusters of AI chips can require tens of billions of dollars. Companies with diverse revenue and strong credit can still borrow; firms whose entire business depends on AI infrastructure face a tougher time as lenders become more selective.
Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya had earlier said many neoclouds appear poorly funded and badly run. He argued that Amazon, Microsoft and Google are moving slowly on deals and prefer to keep computing power for their own use. He said delays in building data centers could leave many chips and half-finished projects sitting idle or failing to earn enough to cover financing costs in 2027.
Lately, financial markets have become increasingly worried about the payoff from massive AI spending. That has pressured AI-linked stocks and the broader market. Nasdaq futures traded near 29,080 as of this writing, down sharply from above 30,000 early this month.
Diversified RWA stablecoins sustain 5-7% yield from real credit as crypto funding compresses to ~4%. GENIUS pushes yield off-chain; TAM grows to $4B in 3 years.

results.title: MacBook Pro's Switch to OLED Could Spell Trouble for Mini-LED Industry
results.author: Hartley Charlton
results.content:
Apple's expected switch to OLED for the MacBook Pro will help accelerate a sharp decline in mini-LED laptop displays, with annual panel shipments forecast to fall roughly 75% between 2025 and 2027, according to Counterpoint Research.
Apple's MacBook Pro models have used mini-LED displays since 2021, but Counterpoint expects notebook panel shipments using the technology to drop 38% in 2026 and another 60% in 2027. Those consecutive declines would leave shipments at approximately a quarter of their 2025 level.
OLED is heading in the opposite direction. Notebook OLED panel shipments are projected to grow 50% this year and 24% next year, amounting to an 86% increase over 2025. Counterpoint identifies the anticipated OLED MacBook Pro and demand for premium AI PCs as drivers, even as the overall notebook display market is expected to shrink 3% in 2026.
The forecast points to a rapid change in manufacturers' display choices. Counterpoint says OLED's thinner profile, image quality, and improving cost competitiveness are encouraging adoption, with tandem OLED designs and larger production facilities supporting further growth.
For MacBook Pro users, the display transition is also expected to bring touch input to the Mac for the first time. Samsung Display is reportedly the exclusive supplier of the new 14-inch and 16-inch OLED touch panels, manufactured on its 8.6-generation line in Asan, South Korea, according to The Elec.
Apple is expected to unveil the OLED MacBook Pro models on Wednesday, October 28 at its "Pro and tell" media experience in Los Angeles. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the laptops will be significantly lighter and replace the display notch with a Dynamic Island.
The OLED models are expected to sit above the existing mini-LED versions initially, giving buyers a choice during the transition. Gurman says Apple will eventually discontinue the mini-LED models, although the new OLED machines could carry starting prices up to $500 higher.

results.title: IT and security leaders of the AI era must go back to basics and beware the hype
results.author: Henrique Bernardes Teixeira
results.content:
CISOs and CIOs should not just chase the latest hype around AI that can escape sandboxes and morphing security threats, but bet on tried and true ROI of identity security.
It’s demonstrably true that the information security scene is transforming as agentic AI accelerates operational speed and potentially exposes new attack surfaces. Most AI providers have reported their latest generation models are so powerful that they are capable of escaping sandboxes and hacking organizations. Regardless if you believe this is hype, truth or genius marketing, what matters is this: information security leaders should rigorously check the basics of their discipline.
SVP Strategy for Saviynt.
Yes, CISOs need to be ahead of the curve but this can’t be at the cost of dropping the ball on security and identity essentials. I say this because, all too often, even in sophisticated and otherwise mature enterprises, the latest breaches are still abusing the lack of essential controls, via credentials and permissions the agents should never have been able to reach.
And sometimes, thought leaders and experts attempting to understand and communicate rapid technology changes, are creating more confusion and distracting from first principles.
‘AI washing’ – the practice of overstating the importance of AI in a product, project or strategy – is real. We need to do more to demystify data security and separate hype from reality and place a higher value on specificity when we talk about risks.
The identity challenge
The industry's instinct to frame this as an "AI security" problem is understandable, but it is not actionable. For CISOs trying to reduce real risk, the more precise frame is identity.
For an example of what I’m talking about, consider onboarding. When people join an organization, they are granted privileges based on their needs, seniority and roles. A major part of contemporary information security is about staying on top of identity management, but that’s not easy.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
In hypergrowth, companies hire very quickly. But IT leaders also need to stay abreast of many other people who need access to systems. These include freelancers, consultants, suppliers, auditors and work-experience temporary staff. That gap (unrevoked, over-permissioned, forgotten access) is exactly what autonomous AI agents exploited in the Hugging Face breach earlier this year.
The attack was novel. The underlying vulnerability was not. NHIs and human identities share the same failure mode: access granted, never reviewed, never revoked. That is the identity challenge, and it predates AI by decades.
A complex puzzle
IT today is complicated. CIOs stay in their roles for between three and five years. CISOs (and security staff generally) are in high demand, and organizations understandably turn to outsourcers for help. It’s easy for basic management disciplines like maintaining identity hygiene to get lost in the mix, such are the comings and goings of personnel.
And things are getting harder. Who owns an AI identity? Not every enterprise employs an identity specialist, so who is in charge when the identity is non-human? The CIO? What about the CISO? HR? How does the chief risk officer fit in?
It’s easy for tasks to fall between gaps. And even if onboarding is immaculate, who is running offboarding and the impacts on identity? The consequences of that question going unanswered are well documented. Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that exploitation of vulnerabilities has overtaken stolen credentials as the top initial access vector for the first time in 19 years.
But credentials still drove the privilege escalation and lateral movement that followed. A vulnerability opens the door; an unmanaged identity walks through the building unchallenged.
And in the agentic AI era, who will be in charge of managing those NHIs that often have extraordinarily high permissions and license to roam? The Hugging Face breach answered that question in practice: nobody was. One over-privileged, unmonitored non-human identity provided cluster-admin access across two environments the moment it was compromised.
The AI was the intruder. Vulnerabilities have surged as an entry point precisely because AI agents are now extraordinary zero-day discovery engines, finding in hours what took human attackers weeks. But identity remains the common denominator: had proper least-privilege, just-in-time access and NHI governance been in place, the breach would have been contained even after the vulnerability was exploited. You cannot patch your way out of an identity problem.
Back to basics (and learning from the past)
If I think about a lot of the breaches I’ve seen, a lot of them relate to these seemingly obvious gaps that become chasms. It’s the left- behind orphan credentials, the ‘puppies with two owners’ and other grey areas that cause problems. ‘Hey. I thought you had this?’, people hear… when it’s too late.
To improve, we need to learn from the past, because we all know the famous quote (of uncertain authorship) about those who ignore history being condemned to repeat mistakes.
A relevant analogy here is cloud computing. Some of us lived through the datacenter wave, then the cloud wave hit. The Capital One breach of 2019 (over 100 million records exposed through a misconfigured AWS role) became the defining lesson of that era: cloud created vast new entitlement sprawl, and nobody was governing it. That breach, and others like it, drove the creation of Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM) to bring least-privilege principles to cloud permissions at scale. AI is the current wave, and the pattern is similar.
Agents are being deployed with extraordinarily broad permissions, credentials are being embedded in pipelines without rotation or scoping, and ownership of who governs those entitlements is unclear. We will need the same focused response we built for the cloud. Not new acronyms, but the same rigorous application of least-privilege, just-in-time access, and entitlement governance, adapted to the new environment. And whatever wave follows AI will present the same challenge again. Identity is the constant.
Every wave reshapes the technology landscape, but the question of who (human or machine) has access to what, under what conditions, and for how long, never goes away. We just keep failing to answer it before the damage is done. If you weren't there, speak to a cloud veteran because so much of security today has to be about assembling teams of all talents. So use them and build consensus with clear allocation of who is responsible for what and a handover plan for when people leave or swap roles.
The current environment is replete with risks. Consider what AI has done to the act of building software: a non-coder like me can now spin up an app or deploy an agent in an afternoon. That is genuinely transformative, and dangerous. The population of people creating software that handles credentials, calls APIs, and interacts with production systems has exploded overnight, and most of them have never thought about identity hygiene in their lives.
Every time you use an LLM, you are storing credentials somewhere. As that population scales, so does the attack surface. We will see an avalanche of badly architected agents and apps built fast, deployed faster, and governed by nobody. It’s easy to offer up credentials to the world just as misconfigured AWS accounts led to major problems a couple of decades ago.
Today, everybody is excited about the abuses of agents running wild. These are hot stories, and yes, we should be concerned. But really, hackers are going to hack, just as they always have, and they will exploit any loopholes we offer up. The Verizon 2026 DBIR showed vulnerabilities are now the number one initial access vector, but identity is what converts a foothold into a catastrophe.
So many foundational security elements remain neglected like storing static credentials in plain sight. We can still do a lot more with Zero-Trust principles and enforcing least privilege to mitigate risks and reduce impacts. The tools exist and the discipline exists. CIEM was built precisely because the cloud created entitlement problems nobody had anticipated, and it worked, for organizations that adopted it seriously.
The same rigor applied to NHI governance and agentic AI today will determine whether the next wave of breach headlines features your organization or your competitor's. Let’s get the basics right and ensure we can walk at the same time as we try to run.

Information security leaders should prioritize fundamental identity management and governance over AI hype to prevent unauthorized access and mitigate risks posed by autonomous agentic AI systems.

### Key Points
- Identity management remains the primary defense against breaches, as unmanaged credentials and permissions often facilitate lateral movement after an initial vulnerability is exploited.
- The 2024 Hugging Face breach demonstrated how over-privileged, unmonitored non-human identities (NHIs) can provide attackers with cluster-admin access across multiple environments.
- Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report identifies vulnerabilities as the top initial access vector, but highlights that identity failures convert minor footholds into major catastrophes.
- Organizations must implement rigorous least-privilege access, just-in-time provisioning, and clear ownership of non-human identities to secure modern, AI-driven software development environments.
- Lessons from the 2019 Capital One cloud breach underscore the necessity of entitlement governance to prevent the sprawl of excessive permissions in new technology waves.

### Why it Matters
Focusing on identity hygiene provides a proven, actionable framework to contain security threats regardless of how rapidly AI technology evolves. By mastering these foundational principles, enterprises can prevent catastrophic data breaches that occur when autonomous agents exploit unmonitored or over-permissioned access points.
